implementation_notes: The Scala thread-isolation bulkhead is a dedicated dispatcher: configure thread-pool-executor.fixed-pool-size = n in the ActorSystem config and pin a dependency's work to it - spawn an actor with DispatcherSelector.fromConfig("db-dispatcher") or run the blocking call in a Future on that execution context - so blocking JDBC or HTTP calls consume only their own threads and never the default pool. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by dispatcher configuration plus message routing; use the sibling effect-semaphore variant when the work is already effectful and suspension is enough.

variants.name: Pekko/Akka dedicated dispatcher with fixed pool size
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala thread-isolation bulkhead is a dedicated dispatcher: configure thread-pool-executor.fixed-pool-size = n in the ActorSystem config and pin a dependency's work to it - spawn an actor with DispatcherSelector.fromConfig("db-dispatcher") or run the blocking call in a Future on that execution context - so blocking JDBC or HTTP calls consume only their own threads and never the default pool. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by dispatcher configuration plus message routing; use the sibling effect-semaphore variant when the work is already effectful and suspension is enough.
pitfalls: Default-dispatcher starvation is the classic failure: any blocking call on the default execution context freezes unrelated actors and futures.
Dispatchers are per ActorSystem and fixed pools oversubscribing the cores degrade everything, so budget the sum of all pools.
Futures created without an explicit execution context run on the caller's dispatcher, silently undoing the isolation.
Blocking inside an actor's message handling serialises that actor; route the call to the dedicated dispatcher instead.

variants.name: cats-effect / ZIO Semaphore
variants.implementation_notes: In effect systems the bulkhead is a functional permit: Semaphore[IO](n) per dependency and sem.permit.use(_ => call) - bracket semantics guarantee release on success, error, cancellation and defects, which hand-rolled counters usually lose; ZIO offers the same with Semaphore.make(n) plus acquireRelease. Use it when the application is already effect-based, since fibers replace threads and no pool must be managed; a dedicated blocking pool remains necessary when you must call blocking Java APIs inside an effect.
pitfalls: Permits must be used through permit.use or bracket; acquire followed by a manual release leaks on cancellation and defects.
Effect semaphores bound fibers, not threads: a blocking call must still run on a dedicated blocking pool (IO.blocking, ZIO.attemptBlocking).
Shared semaphores are created at the edge with unsafeRunSync; creating one per request defeats the bound.
Waiting fibers queue unboundedly, so add a timeout (IO.timeout, ZIO.timeout) to convert saturation into rejection.

Dispatchers are per ActorSystem and fixed pools oversubscribing the cores degrade everything, so budget the sum of all pools.
Futures created without an explicit execution context run on the caller's dispatcher, silently undoing the isolation.
